transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-30
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Riley Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (CTO, Orbis Health), Lina Morales (Senior Backend Engineer), Priya Kapoor (PM)

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API onramp for chat/text generation, focus on streaming semantics, parameter tuning (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and practical retry/backoff patterns. Walked through console sandbox, sample snippets, and next steps for a short pilot. Security and data residency questions flagged for follow-up.

Topics: streaming chunking, SSE vs websocket behavior, partial tokens, stop sequences, temperature/top_p tradeoffs, max_tokens and truncation, retries (exponential backoff, idempotency), console sandbox, token accounting, KV/prefix caching, hosted vs dedicated vs private fit.

Action items (captured in metadata above)

Transcript:
[00:00] Riley: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we got about an hour, i'll kick off with a quick overview then maya will demo the console sandbox and we'll do q&a. Samir, Lina, Priya — thanks for making time.
[00:12] Samir: yeah, thanks, Riley. We're mainly interested in a hosted quick onramp, low latency, predictable cost. also curious about streaming reliability and how you handle retries without duplicating output.
[00:22] Riley: perfect — that maps to what we'll cover. maya, intro?
[00:26] Maya: hey all — short agenda: 1) what streaming gives you in the hosted API, 2) key params and their practical defaults, 3) retry strategies and idempotency, 4) a live run in the console sandbox with a couple of edge cases.
[00:37] Lina: quick note — we have an existing chat service using OpenAI, about 100 qps, and we do some batching on our side. curious about how Redwood's batching and prefix caching would interact.
[00:47] Maya: good call — we do automatic continuous batching at the runtime, and prefix/KV caching for repeated conversation prefixes. it's compatible with client-side batching but often you get better cost/lower latency letting the runtime group requests by token distribution.
[00:59] Priya: can you explain prefix cache — i keep hearing K-V cache and prefix, are they the same?
[01:05] Maya: yeah, sorry jargon — prefix cache stores computed KV cache vectors for a conversation prefix so subsequent turns skip recomputing early layers. KV cache often written K V cache in transcriptions. it's a helpful optimization for chat where users repeat greetings or standard starter context.
[01:20] Samir: do we need a private deploy for that or does hosted do it?
[01:25] Riley: hosted supports KV/prefix caching for multi-tenant, we surface cache hit metrics in the console. dedicated/private can give even more cache warm start guarantees for long-running sessions.
[01:36] Maya: jumping to streaming: we support streaming over SSE and websockets — the payloads are token-level partials, but note that streaming yields partial tokens sometimes due to how tokens are chunked. app logic should handle assembling and deduping pieces.
[01:55] Lina: is there an ordering guarantee? we've had re-ordering with some providers.
[02:00] Maya: yes — within a single request stream order is preserved. if you have retries and you reconnect, you may get repeats, so we recommend idempotency keys and application-level dedupe on message ids.
[02:12] Riley: quick si-de note — common pattern: client sends idempotency_key per user-message; on server side we track result or last token offset so retries can ask for 'resume from offset'. we demo a basic pattern in the sandbox.
[02:30] Priya: what about parameters — temperature, top_p, best_of, max_tokens — what's good for an enterprise chat?
[02:38] Maya: defaults we show: temperature 0.2-0.4 for assistant-style answers, top_p usually left at 0.9 or 1.0 depending on diversity needs. max_tokens should bound your expected reply length; the runtime will truncate older context if you hit sequence length. for safety use stop sequences to avoid trailing boilerplate.
[02:58] Samir: and token accounting? we currently overpay when we stream because partial tokens count twice sometimes.
[03:04] Riley: good question — token billing is per final generated token; interim stream chunks don't double-bill. we provide token-level breakdowns in the console and per-request metadata so you can reconcile costs.
[03:18] Maya: demo time — i'll share the sandbox link and run a sample chat with streaming on.
[03:25] [03:25] Maya: (shares screen) — console > sandbox project > new chat > enable streaming checkbox. here's a simple prompt: "You are an assistant that summarizes clinical notes". hitting run.
[03:38] [03:38] Maya: you can see the stream come in, each event contains delta text plus token index and partial finish_reason when applicable. if the client disconnects, you can re-request with same idempotency key and resume behavior.
[04:00] Lina: i see a 'retry-after' header on rate limit in the console logs — is that per project or per key?
[04:06] Maya: rate limits are per key and per plan; console shows headers in the request log. we also auto-suggest burst-smoothing via the Optimize tab to reduce 429s by adjusting concurrency.
[04:20] Samir: for retries — do you recommend exponential backoff? linear?
[04:25] Riley: exponential backoff with jitter is the industry standard. we suggest small initial backoff for streaming clients (200-500ms) because some infra hiccups resolve fast. for persistent failures escalate to fallback model or queue for later.
[04:40] Maya: also, idempotency keys help prevent double-output when a retry slips through. include message fingerprint and timestamp. we show a sample middleware for express/fastapi in the sandbox repo.
[04:55] Priya: any protection against partial double-outputs when connection fails mid-generation and client reconnects?
[05:00] Maya: yes—two approaches: 1) use resume semantics with token offset so you only request remainder, 2) server side detects duplicate idempotency key and returns cached final output. resume is good if you store per-session offsets.
[05:12] Samir: how hard is it to integrate with our existing OpenAI client code?
[05:17] Riley: typically straightforward — we have SDKs and a Postman collection. most OpenAI-style params map directly: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, presence/penalty keys. function-calling semantics also supported but with different shape.
[05:28] Maya: switching to a quick code example — here's a Node snippet in the sandbox that toggles streaming and sets an idempotency key.
[05:35] [05:35] Maya: // pseudocode
[05:40] Maya: const res = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-chat-1', messages, idempotency_key, stream: true, temperature: 0.3 })
[05:47] Maya: res.on('data', chunk => { // assemble, dedupe by token index })
[05:52] Lina: do you expose token indices consistently across streaming providers?
[05:55] Maya: yes we include a token_index or seq to help dedupe. but caveat: some models emit sub-token fragments; seq numbers help re-assemble.
[06:08] Samir: we care a lot about latency; can you share typical p95 numbers for 'chat-gen' hosted in us-west?
[06:15] Riley: for small-ish prompts (~200 tokens in/out) p95 is around 180-350ms on our hosted cluster depending on model family; we surface per-model performance in the catalog. we can also run a short benchmark for Orbis to get real numbers.
[06:30] Priya: how does batching affect latency? since we do 100 qps, batching can help cost but may add latency.
[06:36] Maya: correct — the runtime balances throughput vs latency. you can set latency SLOs per route; when you prioritize latency the system reduces batching window, which increases cost. Optimize tab gives suggested batch settings for your workload.
[06:50] Samir: what about stop sequences and safety — we sometimes need strict stop behavior when generating patient instructions.
[06:56] Maya: stop sequences are honored in-stream when possible; however partial tokens may still appear until model finishes token boundary. for critical safety we recommend post-generation validation and guardrails in application layer plus our content-safety integrations.
[07:15] Riley: quick competitor note — one difference from some big providers is our console gives token-level cost & latency per request and suggestions via Optimize if we detect cost regressions.
[07:25] Priya: do you have SSO and role-based access for console?
[07:29] Riley: yes — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC. audit logs retained per plan; we can extend retention for enterprise customers.
[07:40] Samir: encryption at rest and KMS — we need HSM integration for keys.
[07:45] Riley: we support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations in the Private product and for Dedicated customers; hosted also supports managed KMS with encryption and audit logs, but for HSM-backed keys we typically do Dedicated or Private.
[07:58] Lina: we have strict data residency in EMEA — do you have regions?
[08:03] Maya: yes region controls for hosted; we can pin compute to eu-west for data residency, and Dedicated can be deployed in customer region for stricter needs.
[08:15] Samir: ok, let's do the live weird edge-case you mentioned — prompt with long context and a midstream disconnect.
[08:22] Maya: sure — i'll send a long clinical note into the sandbox and flip streaming off midstream to simulate drop.
[08:30] [08:30] Maya: (runs) — disconnecting now... reconnecting with same idempotency_key and resume_offset = 120. you can see the stream resumes from token 121.
[08:45] Lina: nice — that resume offset is exactly what we need. how does that interact with cache eviction?
[08:52] Maya: resume works if the backend still has warm KV cache or if the model hasn't been evicted; for long delays a resume may fall back to full generation or cached final output. that's why we expose cache hit rate metrics so you can see eviction windows.
[09:08] Priya: can you run the same example in a high concurrency test to show throttling behavior?
[09:13] Maya: yes — there's a 'load test' tab in the sandbox; we'll run a quick 200-concurrency plan with short prompts.
[09:22] [09:22] Maya: (results) — we see a small tail of 429s; Optimize suggests increasing concurrency quota or setting graceful fallback to smaller model to maintain p95 latency.
[09:35] Riley: that's another pattern — fallback models. policies allow automatic fallback to a compatible, cheaper model under heavy load so the app stays responsive.
[09:44] Samir: sounds useful. what about SDK language support — our stack is Java/Kotlin microservices.
[09:50] Maya: we have official SDKs for Node, Python, Java with examples; the Java SDK includes native async streaming examples compatible with your stack. we can share a Kotlin sample.
[09:58] Priya: re billing: do you support committed capacity or reserved for discount?
[10:02] Riley: yes — Dedicated and Reserved capacity contracts give significant cost savings. hosted is pay-as-you-go with volume tiers and commit discounts.
[10:12] Samir: so for a quick pilot we probably want hosted but with committed predictability for later.
[10:18] Riley: that's common — start hosted, run a 2-week pilot, then move to Dedicated/reserved if the throughput and data controls need it.
[10:24] Lina: security: can we get SOC2 report and your penetration test summary?
[10:29] Riley: yes — i'll share the security slide deck and SOC2 attestation. note some of those docs require an NDA; i'll include access instructions.
[10:38] Priya: what's the expected time to get the sandbox keys and try the Postman collection?
[10:42] Maya: i can provision sandbox keys today, and attach a Postman collection with a few chat flows and the resume/idempotency examples. i'll also include our sample express middleware.
[10:52] Riley: ok, let's recap next steps.
[10:55] Samir: go ahead.
[10:57] Riley: 1) Maya provisions sandbox and Postman collection; 2) Riley shares SOC2 and pricing spreadsheet; 3) Orbis to confirm pilot scope and PII residency needs; 4) schedule a follow-up benchmark call next week to run a short p95 test.
[11:12] Priya: we can aim to start pilot dec 1.
[11:16] Riley: great — i'll send calendar invites. thanks everyone.
[11:20] [11:20] (meeting ends)
